questions.text: Hess's Law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction:

options.label: b
options.text: Is the same whether it occurs in one step or several steps at constant $T$ and $P$

questions.detailed: Because $H$ is a state function, $\Delta H$ depends only on the initial and final states. Hess's Law is simply this fact applied to reactions: split a reaction into any convenient sequence of steps and add their enthalpies.

questions.text: Given $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CO_2})=-393.5$, $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{H_2O,l})=-285.8$ and $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CH_4})=-74.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, the enthalpy of combustion of methane $[\mathrm{CH_4+2O_2\rightarrow CO_2+2H_2O(l)}]$ is:
For $\mathrm{N_2+3H_2\rightarrow 2NH_3}$ with $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{NH_3})=-46.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, the standard enthalpy of the reaction as written is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H=2\times(-46.1)-0=-92.2\ \mathrm{kJ}$ for the reaction producing 2 mol NH₃. Per mole of NH₃ formed it would be $-46.1\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

questions.text: "In a Hess's-law calculation the standard enthalpy of formation of any element in its standard state is taken as zero."
questions.detailed: True. The reference state for enthalpy is the stable element at 1 atm and the chosen temperature, so $\Delta H_f^\circ=0$ for elements. This is why only compounds contribute to the sum.

questions.text: If $\mathrm{A\rightarrow B}$ has $\Delta H=-50\ \mathrm{kJ}$, then $\mathrm{B\rightarrow A}$ has $\Delta H$ equal to:
questions.detailed: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of $\Delta H$ (equal and opposite), because $H$ is a state function and going "back" undoes the enthalpy change.

questions.text: If a reaction is multiplied throughout by $2$, its $\Delta H$:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H$ is an extensive quantity, so it scales with the amount of reaction. Doubling all stoichiometric coefficients doubles $\Delta H$. (Sign changes only on reversing the reaction.)

questions.text: Given: (1) $\mathrm{W+O_2\rightarrow WO_2}$, $\Delta H=-134.0$; (2) $\mathrm{3WO_2+O_2\rightarrow W_3O_8}$, $\Delta H=-131.5$; (3) $\mathrm{W_3O_8+\tfrac12O_2\rightarrow 3WO_3}$, $\Delta H=-66.5\ \mathrm{kcal}$. The standard heat of formation of $\mathrm{WO_3}$ is:
questions.detailed: Multiply (1) by 3 and add all three: total $\mathrm{3W+\tfrac92O_2\rightarrow 3WO_3}$, $\Delta H=3(-134.0)+(-131.5)+(-66.5)=-600.0\ \mathrm{kcal}$. Divide by 3 for one mole: $-200.0\ \mathrm{kcal\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text: For the aluminothermic reaction $\mathrm{3FeO+2Al\rightarrow Al_2O_3+3Fe}$, given $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{FeO})=-63.3$ and $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{Al_2O_3})=-400.0\ \mathrm{kcal}$. The heat evolved *per mole of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$* formed is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H=\Delta H_f(\mathrm{Al_2O_3})-3\Delta H_f(\mathrm{FeO})=-400.0-3(-63.3)=-400.0+189.9=-210.1\ \mathrm{kcal}$ for the reaction as written — i.e. per mole of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$.

questions.text: Using the same reaction as above (overall $\Delta H=-210.1\ \mathrm{kcal}$), the heat released *per mole of Fe* produced is:
questions.detailed: The reaction produces 3 mol Fe, so per mole Fe: $-210.1/3=-70.03\ \mathrm{kcal}$. Always check which species the question references — the same reaction gives different "per mole" values for different species.

questions.text: The standard heat of combustion of butane is $-3151\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and its molar mass is $58.1\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. The heat released per gram is about:
questions.detailed: $-3151/58.1\approx-54.2\ \mathrm{kJ}$ per gram. Converting per-mole to per-gram just means dividing by the molar mass.

questions.text: Adiabatic flame temperature is the temperature attained when:

options.label: b
options.text: Combustion proceeds with no heat loss to the surroundings (all heat goes into heating the products)

options.label: c
options.text: The flame is cooled by water

questions.detailed: Adiabatic means $q=0$ to the surroundings, so the entire heat of reaction raises the temperature of the products: $-\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}=\int_{298}^{T_{ad}}\sum n_iC_{P,i}\,dT$.

questions.text: Burning a fuel in air (with its $\mathrm{N_2}$) rather than in pure oxygen lowers the flame temperature because:

options.label: b
options.text: Inert $\mathrm{N_2}$ absorbs part of the released heat without contributing energy

options.label: c
options.text: Air has a higher calorific value

options.label: d
options.text: Oxygen is a stronger oxidant in air

questions.detailed: The same heat of reaction must now warm up the product gases *plus* a large inert $\mathrm{N_2}$ load. More moles to heat means a smaller $\Delta T$, so the adiabatic flame temperature drops sharply.

questions.text: A simple sensible-heat calculation often *overestimates* the real flame temperature mainly because:

options.label: a
options.text: It ignores the enthalpy of the fuel

options.label: b
options.text: It neglects dissociation of product species (e.g. $\mathrm{CO_2\rightleftharpoons CO+\tfrac12O_2}$) which absorbs energy

options.label: d
options.text: It uses $\Delta U$ instead of $\Delta H$

questions.detailed: At very high temperatures product molecules dissociate endothermically and radicals form; this chemical energy sink caps the real temperature well below the value from sensible-heat-only calculations.

questions.text: The energy balance used to find adiabatic flame temperature is:
questions.detailed: Split into (i) reaction at 298 K releasing $-\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}(298)$, then (ii) heating products from 298 K to $T_{ad}$ using $\sum n_iC_{P,i}$. Equating the two gives the balance shown.

questions.text: Which statements about applying Hess's Law are correct?

statements.text: Enthalpies at the *same* temperature may be added directly.
Enthalpies at *different* temperatures must first be shifted to a common temperature.
A reaction may be reversed (changing the sign of $\Delta H$) to build the target reaction.

questions.detailed: All three are correct practice: combine only same-temperature enthalpies (I); use Kirchhoff to shift temperatures first (II); and freely reverse/scale reactions, flipping sign on reversal (III).

questions.text: $2\mathrm{C(s)+O_2(g)\rightarrow 2CO(g)}$ with $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CO})=-110.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The $\Delta H$ for the reaction as written is:
questions.detailed: The reaction forms 2 mol CO, so $\Delta H=2\times(-110.5)=-221.0\ \mathrm{kJ}$. This is the "per mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$" value used on Ellingham diagrams for the $2\mathrm{C+O_2\rightarrow 2CO}$ line.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: In an adiabatic combustion, the enthalpy of the reacting system stays constant overall, yet the temperature rises.
questions.reason: The heat released by reaction is retained within the products rather than lost to the surroundings.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: For an adiabatic constant-pressure process the overall $\Delta H=0$ (no heat exchanged), but the chemical enthalpy is converted into sensible (thermal) enthalpy, raising $T$. R explains why the sensible enthalpy rises, so R correctly explains A.

questions.text: For the reaction $\mathrm{C(s)+\tfrac12O_2(g)\rightarrow CO(g)}$ where $\Delta n_{\text{gas}}=1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$, the relation between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ at temperature $T$ is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_{\text{gas}}RT$ with $\Delta n_{\text{gas}}=+\tfrac12$, so $\Delta H=\Delta U+\tfrac12RT$. Gas is produced, so the $PV$ term rises.

questions.text: The standard enthalpy of solution of a substance depends strongly on:

options.label: b
options.text: The final concentration of the solution

questions.detailed: Dissolution enthalpy varies with concentration because solute–solute and solute–solvent interactions change as the solution is diluted. "Integral" heats of solution are therefore quoted for a specified final concentration.

questions.text: Given $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CaO})=-635$, $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CO_2})=-393.5$, $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CaCO_3})=-1207\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, the enthalpy of calcination $\mathrm{CaCO_3\rightarrow CaO+CO_2}$ is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H=[(-635)+(-393.5)]-(-1207)=(-1028.5)+1207=+178.5\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Positive (endothermic): limestone decomposition requires heat — the basis of the calcination step in a lime kiln.

questions.text: Which quantity must you *not* assume zero when using standard tables?
questions.detailed: Elements have $\Delta H_f^\circ=\Delta G_f^\circ=0$ by convention, but their *absolute* entropy $S^\circ\neq0$ (Third Law). Forgetting this is the biggest trap in entropy-of-reaction problems.

questions.text: For $\mathrm{C_2H_2+2.5O_2\rightarrow 2CO_2+H_2O(g)}$ with $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{C_2H_2})=+226.7$, $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{CO_2})=-393.5$, $\Delta H_f^\circ(\mathrm{H_2O,g})=-241.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}$ is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H=[2(-393.5)+(-241.8)]-[226.7]=(-1028.8)-226.7=-1255.5\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Acetylene's strongly *positive* heat of formation makes its combustion unusually energetic — the basis of oxy-acetylene welding.

questions.text: If $-\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}=1{,}000\ \mathrm{kJ}$ and the product stream has $\Sigma n_iC_{P,i}=250\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the adiabatic flame temperature rise above 298 K (neglecting $C_P$ variation) is roughly:
questions.detailed: $\Delta T\approx\dfrac{-\Delta H_{\text{rxn}}}{\sum n_iC_{P,i}}=\dfrac{1{,}000{,}000}{250}=4000\ \mathrm{K}$ above 298 K. This linear estimate uses a constant average $C_P$.

questions.text: Which of the following is a correct statement of a standard state for a gas?

options.label: a
options.text: The real gas at its critical pressure

options.label: b
options.text: The pure ideal gas at 1 atm (fugacity = 1)

questions.detailed: For gases, the standard state is the hypothetical ideal gas at unit fugacity, i.e. effectively 1 atm. Non-ideal behaviour is handled separately via fugacity.

questions.text: Regarding the adiabatic flame temperature of a fixed fuel:

statements.text: It is highest for a stoichiometric fuel–oxygen mixture.
Excess air lowers it because extra inert gas must be heated.
Using oxygen instead of air raises it.

questions.detailed: All three hold. Near stoichiometry the released heat is spread over the fewest moles of product (I); excess air adds inert load (II); and pure oxygen removes the nitrogen ballast entirely (III), giving the highest flame temperature.

questions.text: The magnitude of $\Delta H$ for a reaction is independent of:

options.label: a
options.text: The temperature at which it is evaluated

options.label: b
options.text: The physical state (allotrope/phase) of the reactants

questions.detailed: A catalyst only changes the *rate* (kinetics), not the enthalpy change between given initial and final states (thermodynamics). Temperature, phase/allotrope and stoichiometry all do affect $\Delta H$.
